\[
\boxed{T(k,m,n)=\begin{cases}
k+m+n, & kmn=0,\\[4pt]
k+m+n+\dfrac{9\,k\,m\,n}{4\,(k+m+n)}, & kmn>0.
\end{cases}}
\]

**Derivation.** Write \(k=2a,\;m=2b,\;n=2c\) with \(a,b,c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and set \(U(a,b,c)=T(2a,2b,2c)\). Then \(U=2(a+b+c)\) when \(abc=0\), and for \(a,b,c>0\)
\[
U(a,b,c)=3+\frac16\!\!\sum_{\text{6 neighbors}}U,
\]
where a neighbor is obtained by adding \(1\) to one coordinate and subtracting \(1\) from another. All six neighbors preserve \(s=a+b+c\).

Write \(U=2s+f\). Then \(f=0\) on the boundary \(abc=0\) and
\[
f=3+\frac16\sum_{\text{neighbors}}f.
\]
For the product \(abc\), a direct expansion over the six neighbors gives
\[
\frac16\sum_{\text{neighbors}}(abc)=abc-\frac{s}{3}.
\]
Hence \(f=\dfrac{9abc}{s}\) satisfies \(f- \text{average}(f)=3\) and the boundary condition. On each fixed-\(s\) level the interior is a finite connected graph with Dirichlet data, so by the discrete maximum principle this solution is unique.

Returning to \(k,m,n\): \(abc=\dfrac{kmn}{8}\) and \(s=\dfrac{k+m+n}{2}\), so
\[
f=\frac{9\cdot kmn/8}{(k+m+n)/2}=\frac{9kmn}{4(k+m+n)}.
\]
Thus \(T(k,m,n)=k+m+n+\dfrac{9kmn}{4(k+m+n)}\) when \(kmn>0\), and \(T=k+m+n\) when \(kmn=0\).

\[
\boxed{T(k,m,n)=k+m+n+\frac{9\,k\,m\,n}{4\,(k+m+n)}\ \text{for }k+m+n>0,\qquad T(0,0,0)=0}
\]

(Equivalently, \(T(k,m,n)=k+m+n\) when \(kmn=0\), and the same closed form applies when \(kmn>0\).)

**Derivation.**  
Let \(S=k+m+n\). The six neighbours in the recurrence all have the same sum \(S\), so for \(kmn>0\) the equation reads
\[
T(k,m,n)=3+\frac16\sum_{\text{6 neighbours}}T.
\]
If a solution has the form \(T=S+\alpha\,\frac{kmn}{S}\), then substituting gives
\[
\alpha\frac{kmn}{S}=3+\frac{\alpha}{6S}\sum_{\text{neigh}}k'm'n'.
\]
Expanding the six products,
\[
\sum_{\text{neigh}}k'm'n'=6kmn-8S,
\]
so the average is \(kmn-\frac{4}{3}S\). Choosing \(\alpha=\frac94\) makes the constant \(3\) cancel:
\[
\frac{9}{4}\frac{kmn}{S}=3+\frac{9}{4S}\Bigl(kmn-\frac{4}{3}S\Bigr)=\frac{9}{4}\frac{kmn}{S}.
\]
Thus \(T=S+\frac{9kmn}{4S}\) satisfies the recurrence; it also equals \(S\) when any of \(k,m,n\) is zero (provided \(S>0\)), and \(T(0,0,0)=0\) by the boundary condition.

For each fixed \(S\) the interior values satisfy a linear system \((I-P)T=\text{data}\) where \(P\) is the transition matrix of an absorbing random walk on the finite simplex; \(I-P\) is invertible, so the solution is unique. Hence this is the only function satisfying the given conditions.

\]

\[

\]

Try \(g(a,b,c)=\dfrac{3abc}{S}\). A direct expansion shows that for the six neighbours,
\[
\frac16\sum_{\text{neigh}}(abc) = abc-\frac{S}{3},
\]
so the average of \(g\) over the neighbours is \(g-1\). Hence \(g=1+\text{average}\), and \(F=3g=\dfrac{9abc}{S}\) satisfies the recurrence.

Uniqueness follows from the maximum principle: on each finite level set \(\{a+b+c=S\}\), any solution of the homogeneous equation \(H=\text{average}(H)\) vanishing on the boundary is identically zero.

Returning to \(k,m,n\) (so \(abc=kmn/8\) and \(S=(k+m+n)/2\)) gives the stated formula.

\]

**Derivation.**  
Write \(a=k/2,\;b=m/2,\;c=n/2\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(s=a+b+c=(k+m+n)/2\).  
The recurrence preserves the sum \(k+m+n\), so set  
\[
f(a,b,c)=T(2a,2b,2c)-2s .
\]
Then \(f=0\) whenever any of \(a,b,c\) is \(0\), and for \(a,b,c>0\),
\[
f(a,b,c)=3+\frac16\!\sum_{\text{6 neighbours}} f .
\]
Try \(f(a,b,c)=\dfrac{9abc}{s}\). The six neighbours differ by moving one unit between two coordinates; expanding gives
\[
\frac16\sum_{\text{nbr}} (\text{product})=abc-\frac{s}{3}.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac16\sum_{\text{nbr}} f=\frac{9}{s}\Bigl(abc-\frac{s}{3}\Bigr)=\frac{9abc}{s}-3=f-3,
\]
so \(f=3+\frac16\sum f\) holds, and \(f=0\) on the boundary is obvious.

\[
T(k,m,n)=2s+\frac{9abc}{s}=k+m+n+\frac{9kmn}{4(k+m+n)}.
\]
For each fixed sum the recurrence is a nonsingular linear system with the given boundary values, so this solution is unique; the case \((0,0,0)\) gives \(T(0,0,0)=0\).

\[

\]

\[
\frac{9}{a+b+c}\Bigl(abc-\frac43(a+b+c)\Bigr)=E-3,
\]

\]

\[

\]

\[
\frac16\sum_{\text{neighbours}}kmn=kmn-\frac43S.
\]

\[
T(k,m,n)=S+\frac{9kmn}{4S},
\]
which reduces to \(k+m+n\) when any coordinate is \(0\), and the origin is \(0\) by the boundary condition. Direct substitution verifies the recurrence for all \(k,m,n\ge2\). Uniqueness follows by induction on \(S\): the difference of two solutions satisfies the homogeneous mean-value equation with zero boundary, so its maximum (and minimum) on each finite level set is \(0\). Hence this is the unique solution.
